{{Short description|Concept in mathematical analysis}}
[[File:Pompeiu derivative and integral.svg|thumb|440px|A graph of a function (top) whose derivative is a Pompeiu derivative (bottom).]]

In [[real analysis]], a '''Pompeiu derivative''' is a [[real-valued function]] of one real variable that is the [[derivative]] of an everywhere [[Differentiable function|differentiable]] function and that vanishes in a [[dense set]]. In particular, a Pompeiu derivative is discontinuous at every point where it is not 0. Whether non-identically zero such functions may exist was a problem that arose in the context of early-1900s research on functional differentiability and [[Integrable function|integrability]]. The question was affirmatively answered by [[Dimitrie Pompeiu]] by constructing an explicit example; these functions are therefore named after him.

==Pompeiu's construction==
Pompeiu's construction is described here. Let <math>\sqrt[3]{x}</math> denote the real [[cube root]] of the [[real number]] {{mvar|x}}. Let <math>\{q_j\}_{j \isin \mathbb{N}}</math> be an [[Enumeration algorithm|enumeration]] of the [[rational number]]s in the [[unit interval]] {{math|[0, 1]}}. Let <math>\{a_j\}_{j \isin \N}</math> be [[positive real numbers]] with <math>\sum_j a_j < \infty.</math> Define <math>g\colon [0, 1] \rarr \R</math> by
:<math>g(x): = a_0+\sum_{j=1}^\infty \,a_j \sqrt[3]{x-q_j}.</math>

For each {{math|''x''}} in {{math|[0, 1]}}, each term of the series is less than or equal to {{math|''a''<sub>''j''</sub>}} in [[absolute value]], so the series [[uniform convergence|uniformly converges]] to a continuous, [[monotonic function|strictly increasing]] function {{math|''g''(''x'')}}, by the [[Weierstrass M-test|Weierstrass {{mvar|M}}-test]]. Moreover, it turns out that the function {{mvar|g}} is differentiable, with
:<math>g'(x) := \frac{1}{3} \sum_{j=1}^\infty \frac{a_j}{\sqrt[3]{(x-q_j)^2}}>0,</math>

at every point where the sum is finite; also, at all other points, in particular,  at each of the {{math|''q''<sub>''j''</sub>}}, one has {{math|''g''′(''x'') :{{=}} +∞}}. Since the [[image (function)|image]] of {{mvar|g}} is a [[Interval_(mathematics)#Definitions|closed bounded interval]] with left endpoint
:<math>g(0) = a_0-\sum_{j=1}^\infty \,a_j \sqrt[3]{q_j},</math>

up to the choice of <math>a_0</math>, we can assume <math>g(0)=0</math> and up to the choice of a multiplicative factor we can assume that {{mvar|g}} maps the interval {{math|[0, 1]}} [[surjective function|onto]] itself. Since {{mvar|g}} is strictly increasing it is [[injective]], and hence a [[homeomorphism]]; and by the theorem of differentiation of the [[inverse function]], its inverse {{math|''f'' :{{=}} ''g''<sup>−1</sup>}} has a finite derivative at every point, which vanishes at least at the points <math>\{g(q_j)\}_{j \isin \mathbb{N}}.</math> These form a dense subset of {{math|[0, 1]}} (actually, it vanishes in many other points; see below).

==Properties==
* It is known that the zero-set of a derivative of any everywhere differentiable function (and more generally, of any [[Baire_function#Baire_class_1|Baire class one]] function) is a [[Gδ set|{{math|''G<sub>δ</sub>''}} subset]] of the real line. By definition, for any Pompeiu function, this set is a ''dense'' {{math|''G<sub>δ</sub>''}} set; therefore  it is a  [[residual set]]. In particular, it possesses [[uncountably]] many points.
* A [[linear combination]] {{math|''af''(''x'') + ''bg''(''x'')}} of Pompeiu functions is a derivative, and vanishes on the set {{math|{ ''f'' {{=}} 0} ∩ {''g'' {{=}} 0<nowiki>}</nowiki>}}, which is a dense <math>G_{\delta}</math> set by the [[Baire category theorem]]. Thus, Pompeiu functions form a [[vector space]] of functions.
* A limit function of a [[uniform convergence|uniformly convergent]] [[sequence]] of Pompeiu derivatives is a Pompeiu derivative. Indeed, it is a derivative, due to the theorem of limit under the sign of derivative. Moreover, it vanishes in the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the zero sets of the functions of the sequence: since these are dense {{math|''G''<sub>''δ''</sub>}} sets, the zero set of the limit function is also dense.
* As a consequence, the [[class (set theory)|class]] {{math|''E''}} of all [[bounded function|bounded]] Pompeiu derivatives on an interval {{math|[''a'', ''b'']}} is a ''closed'' [[linear subspace]] of the [[Banach space]] of all bounded functions under the uniform distance (hence, it is a Banach space).
*Pompeiu's above construction of a ''positive'' function is a rather peculiar example of a Pompeiu's function: a theorem of Weil states that ''generically'' a Pompeiu derivative assumes both positive and negative values in dense sets, in the precise meaning that such functions constitute a residual set of the Banach space&nbsp;{{math|''E''}}.
